newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Cell phone locator awaits $5 bln market.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Cell phone locator awaits $5 bln market.

text.p: The nation's only maker of a device to locate persons making 911 emergency phone calls on cell phones expects to sell its first units to state and local public safety agencies by the year end, its general manager said Wednesday.
With a successful live trial under its belt and a $5 billion, federally mandated market before it, TruePosition Inc vice president and general manager Louis Stilp said, "it's now just a sales issue."

The product Stilp patented, TruePosition Wireless Location System, is already in production and sits alone -- for now -- awaiting the huge public safety agency market to unfold over the next five years, Stilp told Reuters in an interview.

TruePosition, a unit of the Associated Group Inc, manufactures a system that attaches to cellular telephone towers and assists public safety officials in locating cell phone users who place 911 emergency calls.

At present, 911 operators and emergency response personnel often have difficulty locating a distressed caller because, unlike landline calls, there is no mechanism that records the cell phone number or indicates where the call is originating.
Last July, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission took steps the rectify that, ordering states to instal locator systems like TruePosition's in two phases over five years.
The first, to be installed over the current year, mandates that systems be able to record the caller's number and the specific transponder tower that relayed the call.
The second, to be online within five years, requires the systems to be able to pinpoint the caller's location to within a radius of about 400 feet at least 67 percent of the time.
The company's competitors are more than a year behind TruePosition, Stilp said.
On Tuesday, New Jersey officials touted as a success the results of a 100-day live trial of the system in four southern counties.
Stilp said New Jersey is a top candidate for the first system. Texas, which conducted a successful two-week demonstration in December, is also looking closely at TruePosition systems.

To operate at optimum efficiency, Stilp said the locaters need to be fixed to between 80 percent and 100 percent of an area's cell tower sites. There are about 25,000 to 30,000 cell sites nationwide, he said. The Jersey trial located systems at 55 percent of sites, which he said is not adequate.

The cost for implementing the systems is expected to be passed onto cell phone users as local or state surcharges to their monthly cell phone bills, Stilp said. The average charge is expected to be between $0.75 and $1.25 per month.
